analysis.one_liner: Fast-tracks federal permitting by weakening environmental review, water protections, and species safeguards.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2023 by Sen. Capito with 12 Republican cosponsors, the bill died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The RESTART Act would rewrite several bedrock environmental laws to speed up federal approvals of energy and infrastructure projects. It sets strict deadlines for environmental reviews, cuts page limits, narrows what projects must even be reviewed, sharply limits the public's ability to comment and to sue, blocks agencies from weighing the social cost of greenhouse gases, loosens Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act permitting, speeds up Endangered Species Act consultations, and orders expedited completion of the Mountain Valley Pipeline. It never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Energy companies, pipeline developers, and large project sponsors. They would get legally binding deadlines that force approvals even if an agency misses them, shorter and thinner environmental studies, the right to draft their own environmental documents, sharply limited court challenges, and looser air and water permitting for existing facilities.

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives agencies two years to finish an environmental impact statement and one year for an environmental assessment, and if the deadline passes, the review is 'deemed fulfilled' and cannot be challenged in court [S3].
Project sponsors — the companies building the project — may prepare their own environmental documents, with the agency only independently evaluating and adopting them afterward [S3].

The bill caps environmental impact statements at 150 pages (300 for unusually complex projects), voids public comments submitted outside the comment window, gives courts only 60 days to file a challenge and 180 days to rule, and bars claims against projects that are already built or running [S3].

It prohibits agencies from using estimates of the social cost of greenhouse gases when that use might raise energy costs or delay action, lets existing facilities modify equipment without new Clean Air Act permits, and writes the narrower 2020 definition of protected waters into law [S2].
It establishes requirements to expedite completion of the Mountain Valley Pipeline, a specific 300-plus-mile gas pipeline running through West Virginia and Virginia [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Communities that live near major projects, people who drink water fed by small streams and wetlands, and anyone who relies on the ability to challenge a project's environmental impacts in court. Agencies that miss a deadline would have their reviews deemed complete with no recourse.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near projects and downstream water users

drawbacks.text: If an agency blows a deadline, the bill deems the environmental review fulfilled and shields the result from judicial review, so a rushed or skipped review could not be fixed in court [S3].

The bill rewrites the definition of 'waters of the United States' to exclude groundwater, ephemeral streams, and many wetlands that feed larger waterways, shrinking the reach of federal water pollution protections [S3].
Public comments and objections filed outside the designated window would be forfeited and could not be grounds for a lawsuit [S3].
The ban on using social-cost-of-carbon estimates would prevent agencies from weighing climate damage when deciding whether to approve fossil fuel projects [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Permitting delays for infrastructure are a real problem, and a genuine reform could trim timelines while protecting public input. This bill instead shifts almost every trade-off toward project sponsors: thinner studies, mandatory approvals after missed deadlines, forfeited comments, near-shut courthouse doors, and a special fast-track for one named pipeline. The costs — weaker pollution review and less recourse for affected communities — would land on the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced in May 2023, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Shelley Moore Capito introduced the bill on May 4, 2023, joined by nine other Republican senators as original cosponsors [S3].
Twelve Republicans in total cosponsored the bill — 12 of the Senate's 49 Republicans [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, which was its only action in two years [S5].
No Democratic senators cosponsored the bill, and it never left committee before the 118th Congress ended [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a new benefit from the outcome. Because the bill died without a vote, the existing environmental review and permitting laws stayed exactly as they were, so communities near projects and energy developers alike remain under the status quo.

for.name: Sen. Shelley Moore Capito
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited nine Republican colleagues as original cosponsors.

against.name: Sen. Tom Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee where the bill was referred; no hearing or markup was ever scheduled, and the bill expired in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrats signed on; the Democratic-led committee took no action, so support never crossed party lines.

industries.note: The bill would exempt facility modifications from Clean Air Act permits, ban weighing the social cost of carbon, limit states' water quality certifications, and order expedited completion of the Mountain Valley Pipeline. Faster approvals and fewer lawsuits mean more pipeline and fossil infrastructure, with the pollution and climate risks shifted to the public.

Binding review deadlines that auto-approve on missed dates, shorter documents, sponsor-drafted reviews, and narrowed water definitions cut their costs and timelines. The savings come largely from weaker environmental review and public recourse.

Faster permitting and single environmental documents would also shorten timelines for wind, solar, and transmission projects that much of the public supports. But the same limits on judicial review and community input apply to every project, and the social-cost ban undercuts the climate case for renewables.

The narrowed definition of protected waters would exempt prior converted cropland, artificial ponds, and ephemeral features from federal permitting. Farmers gain regulatory relief while wetlands and downstream waters lose protection.
